query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, introducing a controlled dispersion of nanoscale refractory oxide particles (e.g., Y2O3) will improve elevated‐temperature mechanical properties compared to an otherwise identical alloy without such dispersoids.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (each within 5–35 at%) along with at least three additional elements, processed conventionally without an oxide dispersion treatment.
generation.intervention: Add a small, controlled amount of a refractory oxide (for example, 1–2 at% Y2O3) into the powder mix followed by powder metallurgy and optimized thermomechanical processing to ensure a uniform, nanoscale dispersion of oxide particles throughout the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) under tensile and creep loading conditions representative of extreme service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed nanoscale oxide particles located at grain boundaries and within the grains.
generation.mechanism: The finely dispersed oxide particles are expected to impede dislocation motion and restrict grain boundary sliding as well as inhibit grain growth or coarsening at high temperature, thereby enhancing yield strength and lowering creep rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxide-dispersion strengthened alloy should exhibit a measurable improvement—potentially on the order of 15–25% higher yield strength and reduced creep rates at elevated temperatures—compared to the baseline alloy without oxide additions.
generation.baseline: Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy manufactured without the intentional introduction of oxide dispersoids.
generation.boundary: The alloy composition must conform to the high-entropy alloy definition (each constituent in the 5–35 at% range) and the improvement is expected under high-temperature conditions (600–800°C).
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the mechanical improvement and the long-term thermal stability of the dispersed oxides are uncertain, given the limited precedent for oxide dispersion in primary-Ti/Ni high-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed with the addition of 1–2 at% Y2O3 to create a nanoscale oxide dispersion, and a control set processed identically but without oxide addition. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile and creep tests) at 600–800°C. Use transmission electron microscopy to verify the dispersion and stability of the oxides after testing.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, oxide particle stability via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the oxide-dispersion samples do not show a statistically significant increase (e.g., less than approximately 15% improvement) in yield strength and/or do not demonstrate lower creep rates relative to the baseline alloy, or if microstructural analysis indicates that the oxide particles coarsened or failed to remain uniformly dispersed during high-temperature exposure.
